paper_title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $π_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate future robot actions from visual observations and language instructions (Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026). Their architectures differ, but they share flow-matching action generator that iteratively transforms Gaussian noise into sequence of future actions, called action chunk (Jing et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a; Lu et al., 2026). In models such as π0.5 (Intelligence et al., 2025) and SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025), this generator is implemented as dedicated Transformer module called the action expert, conditioned on features from vision-language model (VLM). Thanks to this , the robot can plan and execute several coherent steps without calling the model after every action. Yet the whole chunk is predicted from one observation, so environmental changes can make later actions inaccurate. To limit this error accumulation, receding-horizon execution runs only short prefix, then observes and replans (Zhao et al., 2023; Jing et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2026). The price of this feedback is fresh start: the unexecuted remainder, or action tail (Huang et al., 2026), is discarded, and the next chunk starts again from Gaussian noise. fresh start may waste completed computation. The action tail has already undergone denoising and overlaps in time with the actions needed in the next inference round, so it may be better starting point than fresh Gaussian noise. Yet the tail was generated from an earlier observation and may have become stale. It is neither ready-to-execute plan nor fresh noise: its value as starting point depends on how much the environment has changed. This tension raises compelling question: Can we exploit the action tail to generate new actions faster without sacrificing action accuracy? We probe this possibility on π0.5 and SmolVLA (Section 2). On LIBERO and MetaWorld, tail initialization matches or improves the action error of 10-step Gaussian baseline in four denoising steps for π0.5 and six for SmolVLA (Figure 2). Yet no fixed short budget suits every sample: the sample-wise optimal step counts span the full range from 1 to 10 for both models (Figure 3). The question is therefore not simply whether to reuse the tail, but how much to trust it under each new observation. Figure 1 VLA-Rolling reuses rather than discards action tails. Confidence controls both how strongly inherited actions are renoised and how many denoising steps refine the next chunk. To adapt reuse to each new observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, three-stage inference framework (Figure 1). First, action-tail inheritance aligns unexecuted actions with the next planning window, using completed denoising work as the starting point for new prediction. Second, lightweight action confidence estimator predicts the reuse value of each inherited action from the new observation and state change. We train it offline on temporally adjacent demonstrations: smaller error between an inherited action and its aligned demonstrated action yields higher confidence target, while the loss penalizes overestimated confidence more heavily. Third, confidence-guided refinement injects more noise into low-confidence actions and assigns more denoising steps when the chunk contains an unreliable action. The underlying VLA remains frozen. To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) Action-Tail Reuse Potential (Section 2): We reveal that discarded tails retain transferable denoising progress: four steps for π0.5 and six for SmolVLA match 10-step Gaussian baseline. Yet the sample-wise optimal budgets span 110 steps, exposing both the opportunity for reuse and the need to adapt it to each new observation. (2) Confidence-Guided Rolling Reuse (Section 3): We propose VLA-Rolling, lightweight inference framework that learns per-action reuse confidence from temporally adjacent demonstrations. This confidence jointly controls how much of each inherited action to retain and how many denoising steps to allocate, preserving useful motion while correcting stale predictions without retraining the base VLA. (3) Extensive Experiments and Analysis (Section 4): On π0.5, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 across LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference time in all 16 pairs, achieving up to 1.48 speedup (32.52% lower cost), and improves success in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. Ablations expose the risk of naive reuse, while real-world target changes trigger additional refinement.

sections.title: 2 Probing the Feasibility of Action Tail Reuse
sections.content: Flow-matching VLA jointly predicts an H-step action chunk from single environment state st. However, during the execution of the action chunk, the latest observations from the environment are not used to update the action, causing all subsequent actions to be based on the state observed before execution began. Errors in early actions cause deviation between the actual state of the robot and the environment and the state expected by the remaining predicted actions, and this state mismatch propagates to subsequent actions, gradually accumulating throughout the execution scope. Receding-horizon execution mitigates such error accumulation by periodically closing the perceptionaction loop. Instead of executing all predicted actions, the robot only the first actions (where < H), then obtains the updated observations and generates new action block. This execution paradigm consumes more inference iterations in exchange for the ability to use new observations to update actions more frequently. This execution strategy also leaves part of every generated action chunk unused. After executing the first actions, the remaining = actions are Atail = AK:H , (1) which we refer to as the action tail. Under conventional receding-horizon execution, this tail is discarded once the observation is refreshed. However, our statistics show that under the execution horizon of common VLA models, the environment does not change significantly. Observations and proprioceptions have high similarity in nearly 98% of adjacent environment steps. Detail statistical data is shown in the Appendix. D.5. sections.title: 3 VLA-Rolling: Adaptive Action Tail Reuse
sections.content: VLA-Rolling attempts to utilize widely existing but underutilized information: the action tail. VLA-Rolling is inference paradigm that uses the action tail of each round as prior knowledge for the next inference round, as shown in Figure 4. VLA-Rolling are designed into three phases: (1) Action-tail inheritance stage (Section 3.1) is used to retain the action and environment state obtained by the previous model after denoising, which serves as the basis for building the starting point of the current denoising stage; (2) Action tail estimation stage (Section 3.2) uses the trained action confidence estimator to evaluate the retention value of the action based on the environment state and its changes; (3) Confidence-guided refinement stage (Section 3.3) generates the starting point of the action by adding noise and assigns it the corresponding denoising cost based on the obtained action tail and confidence. Figure 4 Overview of VLA-Rolling. VLA-Rolling reuses the unexecuted action tail from the previous inference round by estimating its confidence, which jointly determines tail preservation and the adaptive denoising budget while keeping the original VLA frozen. (a) VLA-Rolling inference. The Action Confidence Estimator predicts confidence which controls its interpolation with Gaussian noise. The resulting initialization is refined using Nadapt denoising steps. The executable prefix is sent to the robot, while the remaining tail rolls into the next round. (b) VLA-Rolling training. Confidence labels are constructed from the quality of inherited actions and normalized with EMA-based quantile statistics.

sections.title: 3.3 Confidence-Guided Refinement
sections.content: To optimize the inference process through preservable prior information in the action tail, we propose the Rolling Action Reuse inference paradigm. The trained action confidence estimator performs forward operation before each subsequent action generation to obtain the confidence of the tail of the current inherited action. This confidence then guides two aspects of action generation: (1) Renoising determines how much Gaussian noise should be injected as annealing before action generation to reduce the likelihood of actions going out of distribution; (2) Adaptive-Step Denoising determines the denoising budget allocated for action generation. The prefix of the action start point is determined by renoising. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We tested on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023), MetaWorld (Yu et al., 2020), LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) and RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b), using π0.5 as the main VLA backbone, and SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 as cross-comparison targets. Our experiments were organized into four parts: (1) Overall performance comparisons showing the models baseline performance on various benchmarks and its performance after deploying VLA-Rolling; and (2) Ablation experiments verifying the impact of different components in VLA-Rolling on inference results.;(3) Analysis Experiments; (4) Real-world experiments verifying the deployment of VLA-Rolling on real-world VLA models.

sections.title: 4.1 Overall Performance
sections.content: Evaluation Setup. The main experiment was conducted on three simulation benchmarks: LIBERO, MetaWorld, and LIBERO-Plus. LIBERO contains 40 tasks devided into 4 suites: spatial, object, goal and long. For each task, we let the model perform 100 rollouts. MetaWorld contains 50 tasks across 4 difficulty levels, every task is evaluated with 100 rollouts. LIBERO-Plus is perturbed version of the LIBERO dataset, incorporating common perturbations such as lighting and background variations, resulting in total of 10,030 tasks. We test our model on every task for 1 episode. RoboTwin 2.0 contains 50 bimanual manipulation, owning corresponding variants with random perturbations to test the models robustness. We ran 100 rollouts for each task. Evaluation Results. Table 1 shows that VLA-Rolling provides significant Pareto improvements, maintaining or improving task success rates while reducing inference costs. From the results, we can make two observations: First, the models inference cost is significantly reduced. The time to infer each action chunk on different models and benchmarks is reduced by 5.00%-32.52%, equivalent to an increase of up to 1.48 times in action chunk throughput. This improvement comes from VLA-Rollings adaptive denoising step estimation, which provides the VLA model with guidance for fewer denoising steps. Second, the task success rate on each benchmark remains basically unchanged, or even slightly improved. This improvement comes from lower action error at each step of action generation, resulting in less cumulative error and an increase in the number of tasks completed. These results demonstrate that VLA-Rolling provides significant Pareto improvements, maintaining or improving task success rates while reducing inference costs. sections.title: 4.2 Ablation Study
sections.content: Table 2 shows the component ablation. We can observe that simply inheriting the action tail reduced the success rate by 4.89%, while merely adjusting the number of denoising steps also reduced it by 4.29%. All the success rate improvements occurred in variants with renoising. From this, we can draw two conclusions: First, even if the inherited action tail is closer to the target distribution than Gaussian noise, we must consider the characteristic that high-step denoising of the action tail impairs action quality (as mentioned in Section 2). Therefore, directly inheriting the action tail and performing full-step denoising will only reduce the success rate. Second, the renoising process can significantly improve model performance. This is because the action itself sometimes lies outside the training distribution, making it difficult to correctly refine it using only the VLAs capabilities; adding small amount of noise can reduce this possibility.

sections.title: 4.3 Analysis Experiments
sections.content: Environment Shift Study. We explored an action confidence estimator model trained using default settings, based on π0.5, and inputting environmental states at different execution time domains to simulate time shifts. The larger is, the greater the environmental change and the further it deviates from the environmental changes seen during model training. Our results in the LIBERO table Table 3 show negative correlation between the drasticness of environmental changes and action confidence, consistent with our assumptions about action confidence in Section 3.2. As increases, the correlation between confidence and environmental changes does not decrease significantly until environmental changes far exceed what the default settings (K=10) can comprehend. This indicates that action confidence estimator possesses some robustness, but still has limitations. Confidence Discrimination Test. We compared the average number of denoising steps for successful and failed tasks on MetaWorld. Figure 5 shows the results, revealing significant difference in the number of denoising steps: across all task difficulty levels, successful tasks consistently required more denoising steps than failed tasks, up to 2.33 steps. sections.title: 4.4 Real-World Experiments
sections.content: In the real world, we used π0.5 on the AgileX PiPER 6-DoF robotic arm to complete our designed target mutation task. In this task, the robotic arm needs to place potatoes into plate. During the task, we will change the color of the target after the robotic arm approaches the targets placement position. The robotic arm then needs to continue the task to test the models response to sudden environmental changes after VLA-Rolling is deployed. Detailed settings are shown in the Appendix. E.1. π0.5 70%(14/20) +VLA-Rolling 75%(15/20) Model SR (%) Cost (ms) 227.28 176.50 Table 4 Model performance on real-world experiments. The results in Figure 6 show that the model initially performs the task of "putting the potato into the blue plate" normally. However, when encountering sudden environmental change, the confidence of the action confidence estimator prediction jumps, indicating that the confidence itself is sensitive to the environmental change. Since decrease in confidence temporarily reverts the model to the original inference paradigm, and because the changed environment is still the same task seen during training, the model can automatically switch to the action of placing the item into the brown plate, demonstrating the practical significance of the renoising process of VLA-Rolling in the task execution process.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper investigates the reuse value of action tails that are wasted between adjacent inference rounds in the traditional VLA paradigm. We introduce VLA-Rolling, which uses lightweight plugin to estimate the confidence of action tail, finding the optimal number of denoising steps to guide the reuse process of action tails. Our results show that VLA-Rolling can effectively predict the number of denoising steps required for action tails, efficiently generate high-quality actions, and reuse the motion information in action tails in rolling manner in each round of inference.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: A.1 Continuous Action Generation In embodied robot control, the VLA paradigm currently dominates (Brohan et al., 2023; ONeill et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026; Pertsch et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Team et al., 2024), utilizing rich visual language and robot motion information to generate actions. Existing paradigms use flow matching (Black et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026) to transfer the priors of the Vision-Language Model as conditions to guide the generation of continuous future actions. However, only portion of the generated actions are executed, while the remainder are discarded to prevent error accumulation. Avoiding this computational waste has become problem that VLA models need to optimize. A.2 Action Chunk Reuse Previous work has demonstrated that information from the actions generated by the model can be used to maintain temporal consistency (Black et al., 2026, 2025; Li et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Sendai et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Oi et al., 2026; Zhan et al., 2026), thereby improving success rate. However, these approaches have obvious drawbacks: they rely too heavily on the quality of the action chunk itself. Low-quality action chunks are still reused as the basis for action generation, leading to incorrect action generation. Therefore, to effectively utilize action chunks, selective utilization is necessary, along with an action-level evaluation mechanism (Jia et al., 2026b,a) within each action chunk, in order to unlock the potential of actions that are discarded from the action chunk. A.3 Efficient VLA Inference Efficiency optimizing paradigm for the inference of the Vision-language-Action Model varies. Some of these works attempt to address the issue from the perspective of model size (Yang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025a; Wen et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a), requiring training the model from scratch. However, recently more work is focusing on optimizing the inference paradigm of action decoder, typically resulting in performance loss (Wang et al., 2025; Pei et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2026; Luan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Tang et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). These methods typically sacrifice the accuracy of generated actions for more efficient generation, and cannot avoid making trade-offs between the two. Few works can be universally applied to existing models and produce Patoré improvements.

sections.title: B Method Details
sections.content: B.1 Details of Model Architecture We implement the VLA-Rolling action confidence predictor as an action-centric Transformer with approximately 30M parameters, while keeping the backbone VLA frozen. The predictor receives the current visual representation and its temporal difference, the current proprioceptive state and its temporal difference, the inherited action tail, and the last executed action. Visual token sequences are mean-pooled, and the current and difference representations are independently layer-normalized, concatenated, and projected to 576-dimensional context vector.Finally, Sigmoid layer is used as the final confidence output layer. The confidence is then used by VLA-Rolling inference rules to determine the confidence-guided noise and action tail-preserving behavior. B.2 Details of Action Confidence Estimator For the simulator environment, we can directly set the execution length of each chunk, thus obtaining an action tail of fixed length. For action confidence estimator, we strictly align the input and output lengths of its model with the deployed VLA model. For the models we use, except for the X-VLA, which uses = 30, = 10, and = 20, all other models (π0.5, SmolVLA, MolmoAct2) use = 50, = 10, and = 40. The actual input to action confidence estimator is of the same length as the chunk size H. Each action tail of length = is padded with Gaussian noise of length before being fed into the model. During the forward pass, an attention masking mechanism is used to limit the models focus to the action tail itself, preventing the added Gaussian noise from affecting the models judgment of action quality. After outputting the result, it is truncated into confidence block of length for downstream use. To avoid having the target VLA model infer across the entire demonstration dataset to obtain the risk quantiles, we made an engineering compromise: during offline training, the q0.1,i and q0.9,i statistics are updated as exponential moving quantiles (EMA) of the valid per-position risks. Specifically, for {0.1, 0.9}, let (cid:98)q(s) p,i be the p-th quantile estimated from the current training batch at update s; we update p,i = (1 η) q(s1) q(s) p,i + η (cid:98)q(s) p,i , {0.1, 0.9}, (11) B.3 Details of Adaptive-Step Denoising We consider the inherited action tail as potential intermediate state of the flow-matching denoising trajectory, rather than restarting denoising from the fresh-Gaussian endpoint at flow time τ = 0. sections.title: C Training and Inference Details
sections.content: C.1 Training Protocal As for the training EMA rate, we set η = 0.99. We use AdamW with learning rate 104 and weight decay 104. In our L1 loss for confidence prediction, we adopt w+ = 2, = 1 to realize the asymmetric penalty. All models we adopted use batch sizes 64 for 4,000 steps. For horizon settings, we use the same default settings as the target VLA model. Training used one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU with approximately 96 GiB of memory. sections.title: Inference protocol
sections.content: Our benchmark tests included LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-PLUS, and RoboTwin 2.0. LIBERO categorized tasks into four types, including long-range and short-range tasks. LIBERO-PLUS, as its perturbation extension, included 10,030 tasks such as camera viewpoint perturbations, used to verify the robustness of VLA-Rolling. Throughout the testing, we used VLA model and VLA-Rolling plugin trained only on the original LIBERO demonstration dataset. MetaWorld provided four difficulty levels: Easy, Medium, Hard, and Very Hard. RoboTwin, as the only dual-arm multi-task benchmark among these, had the highest learning difficulty. During testing, we primarily used two metrics: average success rate as basic indicator representing model performance, and cost as an efficiency indicator, representing the inference time (in milliseconds) for each chunk. The cost, which only includes the model inference time, consists of three parts: (1) the time for the frozen VLM backbone to generate KV cache for downstream action generation, (2) the time for action expert to denoise, and (3) the forward propagation time of the VLA-Rolling confidence prediction. The reduction in adaptive denoising steps decreases the cost of part (2). In our main experiment, we tested 100 episodes per task on LIBERO and MetaWorld, 1 episode per task on LIBERO-PLUS, and 100 episodes per task on 50 tasks in the clean subset for Robotwin. All simulator tests were conducted on four RTX 4090 32GB GPUs.

sections.title: D Additional Experimental Results
sections.content: D.1 Ablation Sensitivity We evaluated the sensitivity of VLA-Rolling to the confidence calibration parameter α on the LIBERO dataset. The parameter α controls the slope of the confidence calibration function, thus affecting how prediction confidence translates into action tail preservation and the adaptive denoising budget. We evaluated α {0.0, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} while keeping all other parameters constant. Following the same evaluation procedure, we tested all 40 tasks on the LIBERO dataset, 10 epochs per task, and reported the average success rate, average prediction denoising steps, and model inference latency per action block. The results in Table 5 show that calibration strength affects task performance and computational resource allocation. Without effective calibration (α=0), VLA-Rolling uses an average of 6.861 denoising steps, resulting in the highest inference latency of 206.7 ms/block, with success rate of only 97.25%. Increasing the α value to 1.0 reduced the average denoising budget to 6.155 steps and inference latency to 187.6 ms/block, but the success rate slightly decreased to 97.00%. This indicates that simply drastically reducing the denoising budget does not necessarily guarantee action quality. At α=1.5, confidence calibration provided more balanced distribution: the average denoising budget remained at moderate 6.332 steps, while the success rate increased to 98.50%. Further increasing the calibration strength to α=2.0 did not significantly improve efficiency; instead, it reduced the success rate to 97.25%. However, overall, VLA-Rolling remained relatively stable within the tested calibration range, consistently maintaining success rate above 97%. Of all settings, α=1.5 achieved the highest success rate of 98.50% with an average of only 6.332 denoising steps, achieving the optimal balance between action quality and inference efficiency. Therefore, we used α = 1.5 as the default calibration parameter in all major experiments. D.2 Ablation on Denoising Step Convert We tested different ways of converting confidence to denoising steps and calculated their trajectory-level cumulative errors. The results in Table 6 showed that, overall, taking the minimum confidence as the basis for denoising steps better meets our need to avoid sacrificing accuracy, so we selected it as the default setting. D.3 Ablation on action confidence estimator parameters We investigate the impact of VLA-Rolling model capacity by varying the size of the confidence estimator, while keeping the VLA backbone and all other inference settings constant. We evaluate three variants on the LIBERO dataset with approximately 10M, 30M, and 100M parameters, respectively. We report the average success rate and its variation across different tasks, as well as the inference cost introduced by VLA-Rolling itself. As shown in Table 7, increasing the estimator size from 10 million to 30 million improves the average success rate from 97.25% to 98.00%, while the inference cost only increases slightly, from 1.267 ms to 1.579 ms. In contrast, scaling the model to 100M parameters did not yield additional performance improvements; instead, it increased inference cost to 1.731 ms. This indicates that moderate model size is sufficient to capture the relationship between inherited action tails and the updated execution context, and further increasing the model size provides limited benefits. It also demonstrates that the effectiveness of VLA-Rolling primarily stems from its action tail reuse mechanism, rather than simply increasing model size. Therefore, we used 30M parameter configuration as the default VLA-Rolling model in all major experiments. D.5 Environmental similarity statistics These statistics indicate that refreshing observations after performing = 10 steps typically does not correspond to entirely different environmental states. While rolling in the time domain remains necessary to incorporate newly observed biases and prevent error accumulation, the high similarity between adjacent contexts suggests that previously generated action tails are not necessarily completely invalidated after replanning. This provides an empirical basis for VLA-Rolling, enabling the selective reuse of information contained in action tails, rather than unconditionally discarding them and regenerating the entire action chunk from new Gaussian noise. Real-World Details E.1 Real-World Experiment Setting In our real-world experiments, we chose to use the open-source pi05-base from Lerobot as the base model, the AgileX PiPER 6-DoF robotic arm as the end effector, and designed target placement mutation task to address the confidence dependence on environmental changes. This task consists of two phases: the robotic arm grasps potato and attempts to place it into blue plate. When the potato approaches the upper plate, perturbation is introduced, removing the blue plate and replacing it with brown plate. The robotic arm must continue its action and place the potato into the brown plate to complete the task. We deliberately ambiguous the language instruction for this task as "place the potato into the plate" without specifying the color, allowing both modes to share the same linguistic prior. We then operated the robotic arm to collect 20 trajectories each from the blue and brown plates as target placement points. First, we fine-tuned the pi05-base model on the target data, and then used the fine-tuned pi05 model as the frozen VLA backbone to train action confidence estimator. E.2 Real-World Training Protocol During real-world deployment, the adaptation of asynchronous execution and VLA-Rolling needs to be considered: the execution horizon of asynchronous execution is determined by both inference latency and control frequency. However, under the control of adaptive denoising steps, our inference latency is not constant value. Since the time consumed by flow matching accounts for relatively fixed proportion in the denoising process and is basically linearly related to the number of denoising steps, the inference latency can be estimated from the inference time of its various components. According to the definition of Table 1, we can formally calculate the inference latency as: Cmax = CF + CV LARP + CnonF Cmin = 1 Nf ull CF + CV LARP + CnonF (14) (15) where CF and CV LARP denotes the forward computation cost of Action Expert and action confidence estimator, CnonF denotes the cost of the rest of parts. Subsequently, we can estimate the approximate distribution of the execution horizon: Kmin = Cmin fcontrol Kmax = Cmax fcontrol (16) where the fcontrol denotes the control frequency. For general models, the upper and lower bounds of this distribution will not exceed 100ms in physical time, making it difficult to generate excessive environmental changes. Therefore, we choose to construct data pairs for training on these execution horizons. Finally, we train for one epoch and put it into use.

sections.title: F Limitation and Future Work
sections.content: This work has limited exploration of cross-environment generalization. Experiments on real robots can be extended to more complex task settings to explore factors beyond environmental abrupt changes that can influence confidence estimation, providing more evidence to explain the mechanism of confidence prediction. Broadening real-world evaluation across additional embodiments and interaction settings is natural next step. Furthermore, the combination of our inference paradigm with other inference acceleration mechanisms is worth exploring, as this work does not require any modification to the original model and has the potential to accelerate model inference in conjunction with other mechanisms.
